passages.happening:
‘Then Job answered’ (verse 1). “Truly then you are the people with whom wisdom itself will die!” (verse 2). He has a mind too, he says, and he knows all they know.

“I am a laughingstock to my friends, though I called on God, and He answered. The righteous and upright man is a laughingstock” (verse 4). Those at ease look down on people in trouble, while robbers live in safe tents and those who provoke God are secure.

“But ask the animals, and they will instruct you; ask the birds of the air, and they will tell you” (verse 7). The earth and the fish of the sea know it too. “Which of all these does not know that the hand of the LORD has done this? The life of every living thing is in His hand, as well as the breath of all mankind” (verses 9-10).
passages.hearers:
All three friends have now spoken once, and Job's reply runs through chapters 12 to 14, his longest speech so far. He opens with sarcasm.

Being made a laughingstock was a serious harm in an honor culture. A man's standing, his name at the city gate and his voice among the elders were central to his life. For Job, who had been honored in public, becoming a joke was another loss. Verse 5 names a common human reflex: those at ease look down on people in trouble, as if misfortune were a sign of weakness.

Job agrees with his friends that God is wise and rules everything. What he rejects is their claim that God's rule always rewards the good and punishes the wicked in ways anyone can see. Learning from animals was a habit of the wisdom tradition (Proverbs 6:6), and Job turns it on the friends. Every creature knows that the LORD's hand is behind everything, including what has happened to Job.

Verse 9 holds the only use of God's personal name, the LORD, in the whole poetic debate. Elsewhere in chapters 3 to 37 the speakers use more general names for God, fitting their setting outside Israel. A few Hebrew manuscripts read God here instead.
passages.later: The same line stands word for word in Isaiah, where the LORD promises water in the wilderness, ‘so that all may see and know, may consider and understand, that the hand of the LORD has done this’ (Isaiah 41:20).
passages.asks: Job's friends had become comfortable judges of a man in trouble. Ask whether you have ever looked down on someone whose life had fallen apart. And ask what the world around you teaches about God's hand that your arguments have missed.

passages.t: Wisdom and strength belong to God
passages.happening:
“Wisdom and strength belong to God; counsel and understanding are His” (verse 13). What he tears down cannot be rebuilt. If he holds back the waters they dry up, and if he lets them go they flood the land. “True wisdom and power belong to Him. The deceived and the deceiver are His” (verse 16).

Then Job describes what God does to the great. ‘He leads counselors away barefoot and makes fools of judges’ (verse 17). He loosens the bonds kings have bound and ties a rope around their own waists. He leads priests away barefoot, silences the trusted, takes away the elders' judgment and pours contempt on nobles. “He makes nations great and destroys them; He enlarges nations, then disperses them” (verse 23). He takes away the reason of the earth's leaders, and they wander in a trackless waste. “They grope in the darkness without light; He makes them stagger like drunkards” (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
This is a hymn to God's wisdom and power, but an unusual one. Most hymns celebrate God raising the lowly. This one dwells on God humbling the high: tearing down, imprisoning, overthrowing, confusing.

Counselors and priests led away barefoot comes from the treatment of captives. Conquering armies stripped prisoners of their sandals and marched them into exile, a public shame Isaiah acted out when he walked barefoot as a sign (Isaiah 20:2-4). The poem names no event, and it would fit many periods. Kingdoms rose and fell quickly in that world, and readers who knew their history would hear its truth.

The word for the trackless waste in verse 24 is tohu, the word for the formless earth before creation in Genesis 1:2. The rulers' world is returned to a state before order.

Job and his friends agree that God rules everything. They disagree about what that rule looks like from inside human history. The friends see a neat moral order. Job sees God overturning the mighty, and it makes their order look naive.
passages.later: A psalm repeats two of these lines: “He pours out contempt on the nobles and makes them wander in a trackless wasteland” (Psalm 107:40).
passages.hard:
Does God deceive people? Job says the deceived and the deceiver are his.

The line does not say that God lies. In context it means that both the one led astray and the one who leads astray remain under God's rule; neither escapes his authority. The Old Testament elsewhere speaks of God handing leaders over to confusion as judgment (Isaiah 19:14; 1 Kings 22:19-23), and interpreters differ on how to hold such passages together with the confession that God is truthful and cannot lie (Numbers 23:19; Titus 1:2). Many read them as describing God allowing and using human error within his judgment, not causing deceit as its author. Others read Job's line as his bleak account of how the world looks, true in its affirmation of God's rule but incomplete.

Either way, the verse's main point is that no human scheme, true or false, stands outside God's rule.
passages.asks: Job saw that the wise and the powerful fall too. Ask whether you trust in anyone's wisdom, or your own, more than God's. And ask what would be left standing in your life if your standing were taken away.
